citing_sentences: In this paper, we propose ChatDev (see Figure 1), a chat-powered software-development framework integrating multiple "software agents" for active involvement in three core phases of the software lifecycle: design, coding, and testing.

We introduce ChatDev, a chat-powered software-development framework that integrates multiple "software agents" with various social roles (e.g., requirements analysts, professional programmers and test engineers) collaborating in the core phases of the software life cycle, see Figure 1.

abstract: Software development is a complex task that necessitates cooperation among multiple members with diverse skills. Numerous studies used deep learning to improve specific phases in a waterfall model, such as design, coding, and testing. However, the deep learning model in each phase requires unique designs, leading to technical inconsistencies across various phases, which results in a fragmented and ineffective development process. In this paper, we introduce ChatDev, a chat-powered software development framework in which specialized agents driven by large language models (LLMs) are guided in what to communicate (via chat chain) and how to communicate (via communicative dehallucination). These agents actively contribute to the design, coding, and testing phases through unified language-based communication, with solutions derived from their multi-turn dialogues. We found their utilization of natural language is advantageous for system design, and communicating in programming language proves helpful in debugging. This paradigm demonstrates how linguistic communication facilitates multi-agent collaboration, establishing language as a unifying bridge for autonomous task-solving among LLM agents. The code and data are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev.

sections.body: The paper proposes ChatDev, in which software agents with social roles such as requirements analysts, programmers, and test engineers cooperate across design, coding, and testing. Agents communicate in natural and programming languages. A chat chain divides each phase into subtasks, and communicative dehallucination makes agents request more specific details before answering, aiming to reduce coding hallucinations. The authors built a dataset of software requirement descriptions and report that ChatDev improves completeness, executability, and consistency with requirements. Further analysis links natural-language communication to system design and programming-language communication to software optimization.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: ChatDev uses chat among role-playing LLM agents, with language as the shared medium, across design, coding, and testing.

sections.body: The related work reviews LLMs with role-playing ability and autonomous agents that use memory, planning, and tool use. It describes software development as a multi-expert process, with requirement analysis and design in natural language and development and debugging in programming languages. Many studies apply deep learning to individual waterfall phases such as design, coding, and testing. The authors argue these methods stay separate from one another, which motivates a single language-based design for all phases.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work covers LLM agents and deep learning applied to single waterfall phases, which the authors say remain isolated.

sections.body: Each subtask runs a multi-turn dialogue between an instructor and an assistant until they reach consensus, and the solution is extracted as text or code. The chat chain runs phases in sequence, and solutions from earlier phases pass forward as long-term memory. Short-term memory keeps the dialogue within one phase, with an upper limit on communications. Agents are set up with inception prompts and role assignments through system messages. In communicative dehallucination, the assistant asks the instructor for specific details, such as the exact name of an external dependency, before giving a final response.
sections.heading: ChatDev
sections.headline: ChatDev pairs an instructor agent and an assistant agent per subtask, linked by a chat chain and dehallucination rules.

sections.body: Table 1 averages completeness, executability, consistency, and quality over 1,200 task prompts, and marks baseline differences as statistically significant at p of 0.05 or below. Table 2 reports pairwise win rates judged by GPT-4 and by human participants. Table 3 shows that the multi-agent ChatDev run takes longer and uses more tokens than the single-agent GPT-Engineer run, but produces more code files and lines. Quality is computed by multiplying completeness, executability, and consistency. The ablation and communication analyses are reported in the same section.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: ChatDev scores highest on all four metrics and wins most pairwise comparisons against GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT.

sections.body: The conclusion states that ChatDev integrates the fragmented waterfall phases into one communication system, using a chat chain to organize communication targets and dehallucination to resolve coding hallucinations. The authors say the results show the framework's superiority and the benefits of multi-turn communication for software optimization. They hope the findings advance LLM agents toward greater autonomy and broaden applications of language. The conclusion adds no new experiments.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Authors conclude that language-based multi-agent communication improves software optimization and supports agent autonomy.

sections.body: The authors state that agents often implement simple logic with low information density and struggle without clear requirements, so the approach suits prototype systems more than complex real-world applications. The paper evaluates only completeness, executability, consistency, and quality, and automated evaluation of general software is complex. Human Revision Cost was not used because manual verification of large datasets is impractical. Multiple agents require more tokens and time than single-agent approaches, increasing computational demands and environmental impact.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Agents need detailed requirements, evaluation covers limited dimensions, and multi-agent runs need more tokens and time.
